items.title: Your brain can't truly multitask
items.text:
Your brain can't truly multitask

You try to juggle emails, texts, and meetings all day.

Evidence: Richard Lee (1960s, Kalahari !Kung): about 15 to 20 hours of focused work per week; Eyal Ophir (2009, UC Santa Barbara): about a 40% drop in attention test scores for heavy media multitaskers

MindLore: how your mind works, from real research.

items.title: Is chasing every extra dollar worth it?
items.text:
Is chasing every extra dollar worth it?

You chase every extra dollar you can earn.

Evidence: Richard Easterlin (1970s, United States): about a 0.2 correlation between higher earnings and life satisfaction; Daniel Kahneman (2010, Princeton University): happiness boost caps after about $75,000 a year

items.title: Why a deadline makes your stomach knot
items.text:
Why a deadline makes your stomach knot

You feel a knot in your stomach whenever a deadline looms, but ancient hunters and modern scientists say that knot is a relic of a different fight.

Evidence: Hans Selye (1936, Canada): Chronic pressure spikes cortisol by about 15 to 20 percent; Michael Gurven et al. (2015, Tanzania): Hadza average cortisol about 30 percent lower than industrial societies

MindLore: how your mind works, from real research.

#psychology #mindset #Shorts #selfimprovement #MindLore

items.title: Pain of Isolation
items.text:
Pain of Isolation

You feel physical pain when your friends leave you out.

Evidence: Naomi Eisenberger (2003, University of California, Los Angeles): Social rejection activates the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, the same region that processes physical pain.; Matthew Lieberman and Naomi Eisenberger (2004, UCLA): The social attachment system evolved in early mammals to hijack physical pain pathways to prevent separation.

MindLore: how your mind works, from real research.

items.title: First Impression Myth
items.text:
First Impression Myth

You judge a stranger in seconds.

Evidence: Janine Willis and Alexander Todorov (2006, Princeton University): Exposure to a face for 100 milliseconds is sufficient for people to form a firm first impression of traits like trustworthiness.; Alexander Todorov (2008, Princeton University): The amygdala automatically evaluates faces for facial threat and trustworthiness before conscious awareness.

items.title: Why Silence Heals Your Brain
items.text:
Why Silence Heals Your Brain

You live in a world of constant background noise.

Evidence: Luciano Bernardi (2006, University of Pavia): Two minutes of silence after listening to music caused a greater decrease in heart rate and blood pressure than the music itself; Mathias Basner (2014, University of Pennsylvania): Noise exposure leads to chronic activation of the sympathetic nervous system and elevated stress hormones like cortisol
